title: Organ context dominates cell identity across a multi-organ single-cell atlas of grapevine
abstract: How transcriptional programs defining cell identity are maintained or remodeled across organ contexts remains a fundamental question in plant biology, particularly in long-lived perennials. We generated a multi-organ single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the dwarf grapevine cultivar Pixie, comprising over 220,000 nuclei from nine organs across vegetative and reproductive development, each sampled in two biological replicates. We annotated 46 distinct cell types and anatomical structures, reconstructed developmental trajectories within selected cell types, and inferred gene regulatory networks at cell-type resolution. Organ identity accounted for 65% of regulon activity variance across the atlas compared to only 17% for cell type, demonstrating that organ context is the dominant driver of transcriptional variation in most shared cell types. Broadly distributed cell types including epidermis and xylem parenchyma underwent extensive organ-specific reprogramming, while companion cells maintained organ-independent regulatory programs across all nine organs, representing the stable end of a continuum of transcriptional plasticity. This finding suggests that companion cell identity is buffered against organ context, consistent with their invariant role in phloem loading. This atlas establishes a reference framework for dissecting gene regulatory network organization across organs in a perennial crop and provides a resource for cell-type-resolved functional genomics in grapevine and other woody perennials.
